content.title: COOKING MISTAKES THAT ARE SECRETLY KILLING YOUR {{NUTRIENTS}}
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – Up to half its vitamin C can leach into the water; steam it for 4-5 minutes instead to keep most of it intact.
**Overcrowding the pan** – Packing too much food in traps steam, so vegetables boil instead of sear, losing that nutrient-preserving caramelized crust.
**Rinsing canned beans too fast** – A quick splash doesn't cut it; rinse for 30 seconds under running water to wash off most of the added sodium.
**Tossing the cooking water** – Nutrients from veggies and pasta often end up in that leftover water; save a splash for soups or sauces instead of pouring it down the drain.
**Cooking oil at high smoke point mistakes** – Using extra virgin olive oil for high-heat searing breaks it down fast; save it for finishing dishes and use a neutral oil like avocado for high heat.
**Salting meat right before cooking** – This draws moisture out before it can reabsorb; salt at least 20 minutes ahead so it stays juicy.
**Peeling everything** – Many skins (zucchini, cucumber, potato) hold a big share of the fiber and minerals; a quick scrub beats peeling for most produce.
**Letting food sit out after cooking** – Leaving meals at room temp for over 2 hours lets bacteria multiply fast, even if it still looks and smells fine.

content.caption:
A few of these mistakes are worth slowing down on. With broccoli, the vitamin C is water-soluble, meaning it dissolves right into whatever liquid you're cooking it in, so boiling for too long is basically pouring nutrients down the sink. Steaming keeps the florets away from direct water contact, which is why it preserves so much more. With canned beans, that starchy liquid (aquafaba) carries a surprising amount of the added sodium from processing, so a proper rinse under running water makes a real difference to your daily intake. And salting meat early isn't just a flavor trick: the salt first pulls moisture to the surface, then over time gets reabsorbed back in along with it, which is what keeps the meat tender instead of dry. Everyone's kitchen setup is different, so adjust based on what you're actually cooking.
